note: 50-minute period. Slides 13 and 14 (energy order, 4s before 3d) and the period-length slide can be cut without breaking the section. Quantum-numbers preview (brief slide 17, optional) left out; it belongs with 2.3.

fields.headline:
2.2
Energy Levels, Sublevels & Orbitals
fields.subhead: Name the levels, sublevels, and orbitals, and say how many electrons each can hold.

imageSubjects.section: a long-exposure photograph of fireflies over a dark field

slides.notes: Section opener. Pacing: 22 slides is the top of range for a 50-minute period. Cuttable if short: slides 14, 15 and 19 (energy order, 4s before 3d, period lengths). Image slot (empty): section: a long-exposure photograph of fireflies over a dark field.

fields.headline: What You Will Be Able to Do
fields.subhead: By the end of 2.2 you can do these three things.
fields.k1_b: Describe an orbital as a region where an electron is probably found.
fields.k2_b: Name the sublevels in each level. State the orbitals and electrons each holds.
fields.k3_b: Link sublevels and orbitals to the block layout of the periodic table.
fields.mustwrite: I can name any sublevel and say how many electrons it holds.

imageSubjects.aside: a hand ticking a checklist on a clipboard

slides.notes: Learning targets, condensed from the four in the brief to three cards: targets 2 and 3 (names, orbitals, capacities) are merged. Matt to confirm the merge. Read aloud, do not linger. Image slot (empty): aside: a hand ticking a checklist on a clipboard.

fields.headline: Bohr Failed for Helium
fields.subhead: The Bohr model worked for hydrogen. For helium and every atom after it, the energies came out wrong.
fields.keyq: Bohr failed for helium. What replaced it?

imageSubjects.concept: a chalkboard with a half-erased circular orbit diagram

slides.notes: Hook. Ask first, then reveal: Bohr failed for helium. Answer to take: the quantum-mechanical (electron cloud) model. Image slot (empty): concept: a chalkboard with a half-erased circular orbit diagram.

fields.headline: Three Words You Need First
fields.subhead: Write these before we go further. Each one sits inside the one before.
fields.k1_b: The main shell. Numbered n = 1, 2, 3, 4, and up.
fields.k2_b: A group of orbitals inside a level. Named s, p, d, f.
fields.k3_b: A region where an electron is probably found. Holds up to 2 electrons.
fields.mustwrite: Energy levels contain sublevels. Sublevels contain orbitals.

imageSubjects.aside: a set of nested wooden boxes, open, on a bench

slides.notes: Three nested words. Students write the bar. Check that they say 'inside', not 'equal to'. Image slot (empty): aside: a set of nested wooden boxes, open, on a bench.

fields.headline: How the Model Changed
fields.subhead: Two ideas replaced Bohr's circular paths.
fields.k1_b:
Described electrons with wave equations.

The math gives probabilities, not paths.
fields.k2_b: The uncertainty principle: you cannot know an electron's exact position and exact momentum at once.
fields.k3_b: The quantum-mechanical model, also called the electron cloud model.
fields.mustwrite: Electrons are described by probability, not by paths.

imageSubjects.aside: a vintage chalkboard covered in wave equations

slides.notes: Name Heisenberg only; do not derive. Probability replaces paths. Image slot (empty): aside: a vintage chalkboard covered in wave equations.

fields.headline: Orbit vs. Orbital
fields.subhead: The two words sound alike. They mean different things.
fields.c1_b:
A fixed circular path.

The electron is on the line.
fields.c2_b:
A region of space.

The electron is probably
inside it.
fields.mustwrite: An orbital is a region of high probability for finding an electron, not a path.

imageSubjects.concept: a long-exposure photograph of a swarm of fireflies forming a glowing cloud

slides.notes: Misconception to hit: electrons do not travel along the orbital outline. Image slot (empty): concept: a long-exposure photograph of a swarm of fireflies forming a glowing cloud.

fields.headline: Energy Levels: the Number n
fields.subhead: n is the principal quantum number: 1, 2, 3, 4, and up.
fields.c1_b:
n = 1
Closest to the nucleus on average.
Lowest energy.
fields.c2_b:
n = 4
Farther from the nucleus on average.
Higher energy.
fields.mustwrite: Higher n means higher energy and a larger average distance from the nucleus.

imageSubjects.concept: a stone staircase seen from the bottom step, lit from above

slides.notes: Higher n: higher energy, larger average distance. Image slot (empty): concept: a stone staircase seen from the bottom step, lit from above.

fields.headline: Levels, Sublevels, Orbitals
fields.subhead: Each box is one orbital. Read the map from the bottom up.
fields.a3_b: d: five orbitals, mostly four lobes. f: more complex.

slides.notes: Read the map bottom up. d starts at n = 3, f at n = 4; n = 1 has only s, n = 2 only s and p.

fields.headline: Orbital Shapes
fields.subhead: These are probability regions. The electron does not travel along the outline.
fields.a1_b: One orbital, centered on the nucleus.
fields.a2_b: Three orbitals: along x, y, and z.
fields.a3_b: d: mostly four lobes. f: more complex.

slides.notes: Shapes are probability regions, not paths. Slide shows one of the five d orbitals; the fifth d shape differs slightly (named, not drawn). f is names only.

fields.headline: How Many Electrons Fit
fields.subhead: Orbitals are the unit. Count orbitals, then double.
fields.k3_b: The 2 electrons in one orbital have opposite spins. Section 2.3 puts this to work.
fields.mustwrite: One orbital holds 2 electrons. s holds 2, p holds 6, d holds 10, f holds 14.

imageSubjects.aside: an open egg carton on a lab bench

slides.notes: Misconception: an orbital holds 2 electrons, not as many as its sublevel. Spin pairing is formalised in S2.3. Image slot (empty): aside: an open egg carton on a lab bench.

fields.headline: Example: The n = 3 Level
fields.subhead: We do this one together. List first, then count.
fields.problem: List the sublevels in n = 3. Give the orbitals and maximum electrons in each.
fields.g1_b:
n = 3
Level n has n sublevels
fields.g2_b:
Sublevels
Orbitals in each
Max electrons
fields.mustwrite: Level n has n sublevels. List them, then count the orbitals.

imageSubjects.aside: a three-tier wooden shelf with small boxes

slides.notes: Do together. Students list sublevels first (3s, 3p, 3d), then count. Work area stays empty for the board. Image slot (empty): aside: a three-tier wooden shelf with small boxes.

fields.headline: The n = 3 Level, Worked
fields.subhead: Check your list against this.

imageSubjects.data: pencil and graph paper with tally marks

slides.notes: Key: 3s 1 orbital 2 e-; 3p 3 orbitals 6 e-; 3d 5 orbitals 10 e-. Total 9 orbitals = n^2, 18 e- = 2n^2. Image slot (empty): data: pencil and graph paper with tally marks.

fields.headline: Capacity of Each Level
fields.subhead: Add up the sublevels and the pattern shows.
fields.a3_b: n of them, one new letter per level.

slides.notes: Pattern: orbitals n^2 (1, 4, 9, 16); electrons 2n^2 (2, 8, 18, 32).

fields.headline: Energy Order Inside a Level
fields.subhead: The answer depends on how many electrons the atom has.
fields.c1_b: Within one level, energy rises s, then p, then d, then f.
fields.c2_b:
One electron, so every sublevel of the same n has the same energy.
Do not carry this to other atoms.
fields.mustwrite: With more than one electron, energy rises s < p < d < f within a level.

imageSubjects.concept: four wooden shelves of increasing height in a workshop

slides.notes: Within one level, energy rises s < p < d < f for atoms with more than one electron. Hydrogen is the exception: same-n sublevels are equal. Image slot (empty): concept: four wooden shelves of increasing height in a workshop.

fields.headline: 4s Fills Before 3d
fields.subhead: Filling order for a neutral atom. Levels overlap.
fields.a2_b: In a neutral atom, 4s fills before 3d.

slides.notes: PROVISIONAL wording: '4s fills before 3d' is stated as a neutral-atom filling order, not as a claim that 4s is lower in energy in every situation. Matt to confirm the wording. Previews S2.3. Cuttable. Label reads 'Order rule'.

fields.headline: Example: Capacity
fields.subhead: Your turn first. Then we compare.
fields.problem: What is the maximum number of electrons in the 4f sublevel? In the n = 2 level?

imageSubjects.aside: a rack of seven small test tubes

slides.notes: Students try first. Work area stays empty. Image slot (empty): aside: a rack of seven small test tubes.

fields.headline: Capacity, Worked
fields.subhead: Check yours against this.
fields.f1_b:
f has 7 orbitals.
n = 2 has 2s and 2p.
fields.mustwrite: 4f holds 14 electrons. The n = 2 level holds 8, which is 2n^{2}.

imageSubjects.data: a handwritten tally on a lab notebook page

slides.notes: Key: 4f = 7 x 2 = 14 e-. n = 2: 2s 2 + 2p 6 = 8 e- = 2(2)^2. Image slot (empty): data: a handwritten tally on a lab notebook page.

fields.headline: The Table Maps the Sublevels
fields.subhead: Block width equals sublevel capacity. Helium (1s^{2}) sits in group 18.
fields.a3_b:
d: groups 3 to 12, 10 wide.
f: 14 wide, drawn below the table.

slides.notes: PROVISIONAL: group 3 and f block drawing convention. The f block is drawn 14 wide below the table, detached, with a border; which elements sit in group 3 (La/Ac vs Lu/Lr) is not stated. Matt to confirm. Helium: 1s^2, sits in group 18, s-coloured.

fields.headline: Why Periods Have These Lengths
fields.subhead: The number after = is how many elements are in that period.
fields.mustwrite: Period lengths 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 come from the sublevels that fill in each.

imageSubjects.aside: a periodic table wall chart photographed at a shallow angle

slides.notes: Periods: 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 from the sublevels that fill in each. Cuttable. Image slot (empty): aside: a periodic table wall chart photographed at a shallow angle.

fields.headline: Check: Level, Sublevel, Orbital
fields.subhead: Questions 1 to 3. Answer in your notes.
fields.k1_b: How is an orbital different from a Bohr orbit?
fields.k2_b: List all the sublevels in n = 2.
fields.k3_b: How many orbitals are in a d sublevel? How many electrons can it hold?
fields.mustwrite: Level n has n sublevels. Orbitals per sublevel: s 1, p 3, d 5, f 7.

imageSubjects.aside: a pencil resting on a blank notebook page

slides.notes: Formative 1 to 3. Answers: (1) An orbit is a fixed path; an orbital is a region where the electron is probably found. (2) 2s and 2p. (3) 5 orbitals; 10 electrons. Image slot (empty): aside: a pencil resting on a blank notebook page.

fields.headline: Check: Capacity
fields.subhead: Questions 4 and 5. Show the count.
fields.c1_b: What is the maximum number of electrons in the third energy level?
fields.c2_b: How many orbitals are in the n = 4 level?
fields.mustwrite: Orbitals in level n = n^{2}. Electrons in a sublevel = orbitals × 2.

imageSubjects.concept: an empty desk with a calculator and a pencil

slides.notes: Formative 4 and 5. Answers: (4) n = 3: 3s 2 + 3p 6 + 3d 10 = 18 electrons (2n^2 = 18). (5) n = 4: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 orbitals (n^2 = 16). Collect or compare. Image slot (empty): concept: an empty desk with a calculator and a pencil.

fields.subhead: Fill the orbitals in order.
